input.text: Ninety kilometers west of Beijing, a whole Ming-and-Qing village sits intact in a mountain fold: Cuandixia, founded centuries ago by a single family — the Han clan — whose descendants still live in its stone courtyards today. The village's name begins with the rarest character in China: 爨, meaning "cooking stove," twenty-nine strokes of homework nightmares and local pride. Built of mountain stone along a hillside shaped — say the feng shui minded — like a gourd or a tablet, its seventy-some courtyards step up the slope in gray stone and black tile, linked by alleys worn smooth by centuries of feet. Filmmakers discovered it long ago; slow travelers followed. Come for a day trip — walk the village spine, climb to the viewing platform for the whole panorama, eat a farmhouse lunch — or stay overnight in a courtyard guesthouse and hear actual silence. It is the Beijing countryside's best-preserved memory, hiding three mountain bends from the highway.
